transcript.text: Bit of a weird one - my son put the microwave on for 10 minutes with nothing in it by accident. Now there's a horrible smell. Is it broken?

**It might be fine, but it's worth checking carefully.** Running a microwave empty is one of the main ways they get damaged, because the microwave energy has nothing to absorb it and reflects back into the magnetron (the part that generates the microwaves). Ten minutes is a fairly long time, so some damage is possible, though many microwaves survive it.

**First, safety:**
- Unplug it and leave the door open to air it out.
- Look inside for scorch marks, melted plastic, or a burnt spot, especially on the **waveguide cover**. That's the small mica or cardboard-like panel on an inside wall, usually the right side. It often gets burnt when a microwave runs empty, and it's a common source of the smell.
- If you see any sparking, smoke, or a melted or charred area, don't use it again until it's repaired or replaced.

**Then test it (only if nothing looks burnt or damaged):**
1. Put a microwave-safe mug with about 250ml (1 cup) of water inside.
2. Run it for 1 minute.
3. The water should be noticeably hot, roughly 30–40°C warmer than when it started.

**What the results mean:**
- **Water gets hot, no sparking, no unusual buzzing:** it's probably OK. The smell should fade over a day or so. Heating a bowl of water with a few slices of lemon or a splash of vinegar for a few minutes helps clear it, then wipe the inside down.
- **Water barely warms, or you hear loud humming or buzzing:** the magnetron is likely damaged. On most household microwaves, repair costs about as much as a new one, so replacement is usually the sensible option.
- **Sparking or arcing inside:** stop using it. A burnt waveguide cover is cheap and easy to replace, but if you're unsure, replace the microwave.

**One important warning:** don't open the outer casing yourself. Microwaves contain a high-voltage capacitor that can hold a dangerous charge even when unplugged.

It's an easy mistake to make, and it happens a lot! Some people keep a mug of water in the microwave when it's not in use to prevent exactly this.

There was some smoke coming out of the vents at the side when we stopped it and opened the door, and it smelled hot and electrical. I've turned it off at the switch but it's still plugged in. There's a brownish mark on the panel on the side wall inside. Is it safe to keep, or should I just bin it?

**I'd stop using it and replace it.** Smoke from the side vents and a hot electrical smell mean something inside overheated, not just the panel you can see. Together with the scorched mark, that points to likely internal damage.

**Right now:**
- **Unplug it.** Turning it off at the switch is good, but unplugging is safer for a damaged appliance.
- Leave the door open and let it cool fully.
- Keep an eye on it for a little while, though it's very unlikely anything will restart once it's unplugged and cool.

**Should you keep it?**
- The brown mark is almost certainly the **waveguide cover**, which scorches when a microwave runs empty. On its own, that's a cheap part to replace.
- But the **smoke from the vents** suggests heat damage behind the panel, possibly to the magnetron or wiring. That isn't something to test at home. I'd skip the water test I mentioned earlier.
- **If it's an expensive or built-in model, or still under warranty:** have a qualified appliance repairer check it before using it again.
- **If it's a typical countertop microwave:** replacing it is usually cheaper and simpler than a repair.

**Disposing of it:**
Don't put it in your household bin. Microwaves count as electrical waste, so take it to your local recycling centre. Many retailers will also take your old one away when they deliver a new one.

And don't worry too much. This is a really common accident, and you did the right thing by stopping it and switching it off.
